title: UAE Paid Swiss Intelligence Firm to Compile Database of “Hostile” Facebook Users
author: Emran Feroz
content:

A private intelligence firm working for the United Arab Emirates compiled a
database of thousands of Facebook users living inside the country--using their
social media activity, including likes of news outlets critical of the UAE--to
identify what the firm described as "hostile" individuals during a broader
crackdown on political expression in the country.

Information about the database comes from a leaked archive from Geneva-based
Alp Services reviewed by Drop Site News. The social media mapping operation
resulted in the creation of a series of spreadsheets with over 11,300 entries
for Facebook users living in the UAE including their names, places of
residence, employment, and other personal information.

The criteria for inclusion in the database--submitted to an Emirati client in
January 2018--included liking Facebook pages published by news outlets and
political groups deemed hostile to the UAE. Documents contained in the archive
show that the firm received €55,000 for the work, carried out under the
project code name "Arnica 2."

The UAE has continued to aggressively monitor social media for any signs of
dissent, with hundreds of individuals
[detained](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/06/gulf-states-more-
than-1000-arrested-in-sweeping-war-related-crackdown-on-expression/) this year
over their online posts related to the Iran war.

The archive was obtained by Mediapart and provided to the reporting consortium
European Investigative Collaborations. Drop Site previously
[reported](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/uae-alp-services-muslim-brotherhood)
on Alp Services' work for the UAE on a planned smear campaign targeting
American Muslims. Other details from the archive were previously
[reported](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2023/04/03/the-dirty-secrets-of-
a-smear-campaign) by the New Yorker.

Alp Services and the UAE's Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to
requests for comment.

The Facebook mapping project began during a particularly dangerous period for
political expression inside the Emirates. In June 2017, amid an escalating
confrontation with Qatar--which included a blockade against that country--the
country's general prosecutor
[warned](https://www.hrw.org/news/2017/06/14/media-blocked-threatened-dispute-
qatar) that people expressing sympathy for Doha or objections to the
government's measures against it could face up to 15 years in prison. Initial
work on the Alp project began one month after this warning.

The Arnica 2 project was proposed to help identify alleged political threats
inside the UAE. In addition to cataloging critics of the UAE's policy toward
Qatar, the project also offered to help target alleged supporters of the
Muslim Brotherhood--a fixation of the Emirati ruler Mohammed bin Zayed since
the Arab Spring.

In a planning document produced by Alp, under the heading "Social media
intelligence to identify hostile supporters in your jurisdiction," the firm
laid out the assistance it could offer to Abu Dhabi in its crackdown.

"Through our team of in-house social media intelligence analysts, we could
identify hundreds of individuals based in your country that publicly 'like'
hostile groups, especially the MB," the firm wrote, offering to use its
"proprietary tools and advanced mapping software," to find "interesting
intelligence and new leads."

Alp identified approximately 1,000 Muslim Brotherhood "supporters" who lived
in the UAE, claiming that many of them were employed at different levels of
Emirati society or in its security services. "Amongst them, we notably find
people who declare working for either the Dubai or the Abu Dhabi police, as
well as numerous teachers, students and other employees," Alp wrote in a July
2017 report. The document, which included personal information about these
individuals, some of whose names were duplicated in the archive, did not
provide evidence substantiating their affiliation beyond likes for Facebook
pages affiliated with the Brotherhood or Arabic-language news outlets critical
of UAE policies.

Alp appeared to treat this research as preliminary work that could be used to
showcase the services it could offer Abu Dhabi in digging deeper to find
possible dissent. "While we already have some preliminary 'raw' findings,
should the topic be of interest to you, we could launch a full-scale
analysis," a representative of Alp wrote in an August 2017 message.

Thousands of ordinary individuals residing in the country are included in
several spreadsheets compiled by Alp for its Emirati client. The lists include
individuals identified by their employment as engineers, pharmacists,
restaurant workers, and others whose only recorded connection to the
investigation was membership in Facebook groups or liked pages.

"We cannot establish what happened to the 11,300 individuals without knowing
whether the database was passed to Emirati State Security and subsequently
used operationally. But given what we know about Abu Dhabi's security
apparatus, I would be very concerned about the potential consequences", said
Dr. Andreas Krieg, an academic focused on the Middle East at the School of
Security Studies at King's College London.

Krieg added that the UAE has an extensive internal security apparatus based on
digital surveillance, intelligence gathering and political profiling. "Its
principal objective is not simply to identify criminal activity but to detect
and pre-empt any form of political mobilisation outside state control," he
said. "A database containing people's names, workplaces, residences and
alleged political associations would be extremely valuable to that apparatus."

In addition to this mass sweep of alleged dissidents found on social media,
some well-known individuals and organizations involved in political and human
rights activism also seem to have been profiled. Among them was a profile
belonging to Ahmed Mansoor, identifying his location as Dubai and past
employment with the Gulf Center for Human Rights. Mansoor, a prominent Emirati
human rights activist who served on the advisory board of the center, had
already been arrested in March 2017, several months before the report was
compiled. The following year he was sentenced to ten years in prison over
Facebook and Twitter posts calling for political reform in the UAE.

## "Strictly Confidential"

An August 28, 2017 working document labeled "client request" listed ten
Facebook pages for investigation, with its search links combining a filter for
apparent UAE residents with one for people who liked each page. The pages
included those for Arabic-language news outlets UAE71, Arabi21, Al Araby,
Rassd, UAE Studies, Emirati Affairs, and Al Dabboor.

Three of those outlets--Arabi21, Rassd, and Al-Araby Al-Jadeed--had also
appeared in the demands issued to Qatar that June by Saudi Arabia, the UAE,
Bahrain, and Egypt amid the standoff between Doha and those countries over the
Arab Spring. The bloc sought their closure, along with Al Jazeera and other
outlets it accused Qatar of funding.

Alp outsourced part of the Facebook mapping project to a subcontractor firm
called Total Trust Investigations, based in Bucharest, Romania, according to
documents in the archive. On August 31, 2017, Alp employee Lionel Badal sent a
contact there seven search links and asked for names and profile information
to be provided in Excel format.

Total Trust Investigations did not respond to a request for comment.

"Some will be so long that we cannot scroll down to see how many people there
are," he wrote. "Obviously, if your IT can develop a small software to do the
job automatically, that would be even better," he added. "Of course, and as
always, this request is strictly confidential."

Badal forwarded the correspondence to colleagues, including Alp chief Mario
Brero, identifying the lists as Arnica 2 material.

In October 2017, Alp's Emirati contact, Matar Humaid al-Neyadi, who currently
serves as the UAE's ambassador to Kuwait, requested and received a proposal
from Alp that set out a 55,000 euro budget for analyzing 10 Facebook pages and
their audiences. Internal records show Alp billed that amount to ARIAF Studies
and Research LLC in Abu Dhabi in December, and delivered the data on a USB
drive the following month.

## Chilled Speech

Alp's internal documents do not establish what consequences followed from the
lists it provided the UAE. But the mapping project came at a time when UAE
authorities were increasingly seeking to prosecute online political
expression.

The crackdown had roots in the Arab Spring. In 2011, with demands spreading
across the region for political change, a group of 133 Emirati citizens signed
a petition asking for the establishment of an elected Federal National Council
that would enjoy some legislative powers. The request was denied and the
government began repressing political dissent of all types, accusing critics
of association with the Muslim Brotherhood and even
[expanding](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/uae-alp-services-muslim-
brotherhood) its efforts globally.

"The Brotherhood has become a catch-all category through which Abu Dhabi can
delegitimize political opponents, independent Muslim organisations,
journalists, academics and civil society actors. Some of these individuals
have genuine connections to Islamist movements. Many do not," said Krieg. "The
underlying logic is guilt by association, where extremely tenuous
relationships are transformed into evidence of a supposedly coordinated
transnational conspiracy."

In November 2012, the Emirati government passed a cybercrimes law that set out
new offenses, effectively banning criticism of senior Emirati officials and
advocacy of political reform. Human Rights Watch officials
[described](https://www.hrw.org/news/2012/11/28/uae-cybercrimes-decree-
attacks-free-speech) the new law as an attempt to ban "even the most tempered
criticism" of Abu Dhabi and its regional policies.

By the time Alp began compiling its Facebook lists, prison sentences for
online expression had already become standard practice. In March 2017, a UAE
court sentenced Jordanian journalist Tayseer al-Najjar to three years in
prison and a large fine over Facebook posts criticizing Egypt, Israel, and
Gulf countries. Later that month, academic Nasser bin Ghaith received a ten-
year sentence on charges that included comments on Twitter about his treatment
in an earlier prosecution. Amnesty International described bin Ghaith as a
prisoner of conscience and
[denounced](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2017/03/uae-prominent-
academic-jailed-for-10-years-over-tweets-in-outrageous-blow-to-freedom-of-
expression-2/) the allegations against him based on his social media posts as
"ludicrous."

In July 2024, dozens of defendants in a new mass trial received life sentences
for their involvement in a political advocacy group called the Justice and
Dignity Committee, which the Emirati government had classified as a terrorist
organization. The evidence, and even the allegations against the group--which
has been described as an independent advocacy group with no involvement in
political violence by Human Rights Watch--has been kept under strict control
by the Emirati government. In March 2025, the UAE's Federal Supreme Court
rejected appeals of the convictions.

The archive of Alp documents does not establish that the Arnica 2 project
contributed to any of these prosecutions. But in its July 2017 report
highlighting the tenuous online connections of teachers and police officers to
human rights and civil society groups, the company promised to work harder to
find evidence that could be used to determine that they were "hostile
supporters" of causes at odds with the Emirati government.

"Of course, further enquiries would be required in order to confirm this
initial intelligence," an Alp representative wrote, "but work is ongoing."
